about: Which GHS hazard pictogram each hazard word in the lab stands for. Chemicals list hazard words in their `hazards` array; reaction hazard blocks name one in `type`. Every word used anywhere must appear here, either with the pictogram(s) it corresponds to or, when it describes something the GHS does not classify, with `ghs: []` and a `why`. The content validator checks both.

source.ref: Wikipedia — GHS hazard pictograms (what each of GHS01 to GHS09 is used for)

reacts_with_water.why: The GHS has no class for reacting violently with water on its own. Every water-reactive chemical here also carries corrosive or flammable, and that word carries the pictogram.

lachrymator.why: Describes an effect (makes the eyes stream), not a GHS class. Every lachrymator here is also marked corrosive, which carries the pictogram.

absorbed_through_skin.why: A route into the body, not a hazard class. The chemical's own toxicity words carry the pictogram.

dehydrating.why: Explains why concentrated sulfuric acid burns, not a separate GHS class. It is also marked corrosive.

unstable.why: Decomposes on standing or warming. Where that decomposition is dangerous the chemical also carries explosive_when_dry, which carries the pictogram.

odourless.why: Not a hazard in itself but a warning that the gas gives no smell to notice it by. The gas's toxicity and flammability words carry the pictograms.

stains_skin.why: Staining is a nuisance, not a GHS hazard. Kept because a student who sees brown fingers should know why.

blinding_light.why: A hazard of the reaction being carried out (burning magnesium), not a property of a substance, so the GHS does not classify it.

molten_metal.why: A hazard of the operation (very hot liquid metal), not a property of a substance, so the GHS does not classify it.

violent_reaction.why: A hazard of mixing particular chemicals, not a property of one substance, so the GHS does not classify it. The chemicals involved carry their own pictograms.
